Imagine a city needing three new pizza shops. We don't know the neighborhoods, only where houses are. We drop three shops, then each house goes to its nearest shop. Next, each shop moves to the center of its customer crowd. We repeat this, moving shops and re-assigning customers, until nothing changes.

This game is called k-means clustering. Its goal is to group data points without labels. We want to make sure every point is as close as possible to its group's center. Lloyd's algorithm does this: first, we assign each point to its nearest center, then we update each center to be the mean of its assigned points, and repeat until stable.

Let's try a simple example with points on a line: one, two, three, ten, eleven, twelve. We start with two centers. Points one, two, three initially group with the first center, and the rest with the second. We update the first center to be the average of one, two, and three, making it two. The second center becomes the average of its points, eleven. Then, points are reassigned.

Remember, k-means always stops in finite steps, reaching a local minimum, not necessarily the best overall. It doesn't find the global optimum. K-means++ helps by picking spread-out starting centers using squared distance. You cannot choose 'k' just by minimizing the objective; use the elbow method. Keep practicing the steps!
